summary:
Brasa is a web app that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent record. MODIS and VIIRS see fires at different resolutions and sensitivities, so you can’t compare their hotspot counts directly. Brasa converts historical MODIS observations into VIIRS-equivalent estimates using a statistical ratio model and a U-Net + MLP ensemble.

You can look at fire activity anywhere on Earth by picking a country, drawing an area, typing coordinates, or clicking a spot on a 3D globe. For each place, Brasa shows fire-history rings, a monthly calendar, long-term trends, anomalies and seasonal patterns. You can put the raw and harmonized sensor data side by side and export the results as CSV.

It’s built for researchers, land managers and emergency responders who need to know whether this year’s burning is unusual and how it fits the longer history.
details:
1. Project overview

Brasa Fire History, Harmonized is a web app for exploring more than 25 years of satellite fire data as a single, comparable record.

Historical fire monitoring has a basic problem. MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and detection limits, so their hotspot counts don’t line up. Brasa converts historical MODIS observations into VIIRS-equivalent hotspot estimates, which gives a harmonized record from 2000 to 2025.

2. How it works

Brasa uses NASA FIRMS active fire data: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra and Aqua) and the 375 m VIIRS instruments on Suomi NPP and NOAA-20. VIIRS on Suomi NPP is the reference sensor, so every MODIS observation is expressed in Suomi NPP VIIRS terms.

Two models do the conversion:
A U-Net + MLP ensemble, trained on the years when MODIS and VIIRS overlap, estimates what VIIRS would have seen before it launched.
A hierarchical ratio model adjusts for differences between sensors, regions and seasons, and for small fires that MODIS tends to miss.

3. Main features

  • A 3D globe showing global fire activity, which you can step through year by year.
  • Fire-history rings modeled on tree rings, where each ring is a year and each segment is a month.
  • A year-by-month fire calendar.
  • Seasonal patterns, long-term trends and unusual fire activity for any selected area.
  • Plain-language summaries, comparisons with past years, and a fire-danger indicator.
  • A sensor comparison view showing raw MODIS, harmonized MODIS and observed VIIRS together.
  • CSV export of the harmonized calendar data and any available raw hotspot records.

You can choose an area by drawing on the map, entering coordinates, picking a country, setting a point and radius, or clicking the globe.

4. Technologies and tools

  • Python 3.12 for data processing and the backend
  • DuckDB for queries and analysis
  • JavaScript ES modules for the frontend
  • Leaflet for the 2D maps
  • Three.js for the 3D globe
  • U-Net and MLP models for harmonization
  • NASA FIRMS for MODIS and VIIRS active fire data

5. Innovation and creativity

Brasa puts sensor harmonization, machine learning, statistical modeling and visualization in one tool. It turns millions of satellite detections into a record you can compare across years, seasons and regions, not just a map of hotspots. The tree-ring view shows decades of burning in a single picture.

The harmonization is open to inspection: you can check any converted estimate against the original sensor observations.

6. Intended impact

Brasa is meant for researchers, environmental organizations, land managers and emergency responders. A consistent record across two generations of satellites makes it easier to spot unusual fire seasons, see how burning shifts through the year, and follow trends over decades, which helps with fire monitoring and planning.
